what: Graham Holdings is a collection of unrelated businesses. Once the owner of the Washington Post, it now owns Kaplan, an education and test-preparation company, along with television stations, car dealerships, manufacturing businesses, restaurants, healthcare services and various smaller holdings.
customers: Varies entirely by subsidiary: students and professionals taking Kaplan courses, television advertisers, car buyers, industrial customers and restaurant diners.
money: Test preparation, professional training and university partnerships worldwide.
Local television stations, the highest-margin segment.
Industrial businesses, car dealerships, restaurants and healthcare services.
moat: There is no single operating moat; the model is capital allocation. Management buys businesses it believes are undervalued, runs them for cash, and reinvests. Television stations have genuine local scarcity value from their licences, and Kaplan has brand recognition built over decades in test preparation.
risks: Only one analyst covers the stock, with a $1,100.00 target below the current price of $1,251.62 — effectively no external scrutiny of a $5.2B company.
The conglomerate structure makes the parts hard to value, and the market typically applies a discount for exactly that reason.
Kaplan’s test preparation business faces structural pressure as universities drop standardised test requirements.
Television broadcasting is in long-term decline as viewing moves to streaming, though political advertising provides periodic support.
Debt of $1.3B against $267.0M of cash is manageable but the businesses require continuing investment.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 11.0 times earnings and 1.02 times sales, which is modest for this collection of assets.
Revenue has grown every year, from $3.2B in 2021 to $4.9B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $5.1B.
Television licences are genuinely scarce local assets with high margins.
The decentralised structure means each business is run by its own management rather than from the centre.
A long record of buying businesses at sensible prices is the entire proposition, and it has generally been honoured.
watch: Book value per share and segment operating results. For a conglomerate, the compounding of book value over long periods is the only meaningful measure.
view: Graham Holdings is what remains after the Washington Post was sold, and what remains is a deliberately unfashionable collection: a test-preparation company, some television stations, car dealerships, manufacturing businesses, restaurants and healthcare services. There is no thematic logic to it and that is the point. The company buys businesses it thinks are cheap, lets their own managers run them, and reinvests the cash.

Kaplan is the largest piece and the one facing a genuine structural question. Test preparation depends on standardised tests mattering, and American universities have been dropping test requirements. Kaplan has diversified into professional training and university partnerships, which is the right response, but the core franchise is under pressure in a way that is not cyclical.

The television stations are the quiet quality asset. A local broadcast licence is genuinely scarce — there are only so many, and nobody is issuing more — and the margins are high. The long-term decline as viewing moves to streaming is real, but it is slower than people expect, and political advertising in election years provides enormous periodic cash flow that the market consistently undervalues.

At 11 times earnings and 1.02 times sales, this is priced at the usual conglomerate discount, and the discount is partly deserved: the parts are hard to value and nobody is looking — one analyst covers a $5.2 billion company, with a target below the share price. What you are really buying is a management team’s capital allocation judgement, assessable only through book value per share over long periods. That is a reasonable thing to own if you trust the record, and the record has generally been honoured. It is not a stock to own if you need someone else to tell you what it is worth.
bull: Capital allocation keeps compounding book value per share while scarce television licences and political advertising fund acquisitions, at 11 times earnings.
bear: Kaplan’s test-prep core erodes as universities drop test requirements, broadcast decline accelerates, and the conglomerate discount never closes.
